notice: Actions and tests are proposals from this skill. Sources do not guarantee product improvements. Load only relevant entries.

principles.title: Selective attention and tunnel vision
principles.claim: What is visible outside the task focus may go unnoticed.
principles.when: A relevant error or state sits far from the active control.
principles.action: Place the change next to its object and keep a signal the person can consult.
principles.avoid: Solving it only with more color or a peripheral toast.
principles.boundary: Position and emphasis do not guarantee detection; attention depends on the task.
principles.test: Complete the task without moderator hints and check whether the change is noticed.

principles.title: Banner blindness
principles.claim: An advertising look can make people ignore useful content.
principles.when: Help or critical alerts imitate a promotion.
principles.action: Integrate information into the journey and distinguish advertising from product state.
principles.avoid: Making a banner louder as the only fix.
principles.boundary: Not every banner is useless; analyze context and meaning.
principles.test: Compare discovery of the same information in task context.

principles.title: Change blindness
principles.claim: A change between states can go unnoticed.
principles.when: Imports, filters, or AI alter existing results.
principles.action: Show what changed, on which object, and what stays; offer persistent review.
principles.avoid: Changing focus, order, or selection without notice.
principles.boundary: Animation can help or distract; a static signal must exist.
principles.test: Interrupt, return, and ask the person to identify state, changes, and next action.

principles.title: Distinctiveness / Von Restorff
principles.claim: Difference can aid recall; translating it to UI attention needs testing.
principles.when: Relevant actions compete visually.
principles.action: Reserve emphasis for task priorities and pair it with text or shape.
principles.avoid: Highlighting everything, relying on color, or turning states into advertising.
principles.boundary: Remembering is not understanding or choosing well.
principles.test: Measure correct identification of the priority without raising selection errors.

principles.title: Cognitive load
principles.claim: Separate necessary effort from effort imposed by the interface.
principles.when: The person calculates, translates, or rebuilds context before acting.
principles.action: Externalize comparisons, reduce context switches, and explain necessary decisions.
principles.avoid: Hiding critical information so the screen looks empty.
principles.boundary: Learning and reviewing a risky action can need useful effort.
principles.test: Record errors, help use, and perceived effort as well as time.

principles.title: Semantic chunking
principles.claim: Grouping by meaning can ease processing.
principles.when: Lists or forms contain relationships that are hard to see.
principles.action: Organize by task, object, or phase and use headings that explain the relationship.
principles.avoid: Creating arbitrary groups of seven or boxes without meaning.
principles.boundary: Groups useful to an expert can be opaque to a beginner.
principles.test: Ask the person to find and explain an item without saying where it is.

principles.title: Working memory: no magic numbers
principles.claim: Measured capacity depends on conditions, units, and task.
principles.when: Someone proposes limiting controls using Miller or the number four.
principles.action: Measure what must be remembered and what can be consulted while acting.
principles.avoid: Using 7±2 or four as a universal maximum of visible options.
principles.boundary: Recognizing visible items is a different task from recalling them.
principles.test: Compare performance with visible context against context that must be remembered.

principles.title: External memory and resumption
principles.claim: The system can keep information the user needs to recover.
principles.when: Long work, comparison across screens, or interruptions.
principles.action: Preserve draft, selection, relevant history, and a state summary.
principles.avoid: Silently remembering everything or exposing private information in another context.
principles.boundary: Persistence needs control, expiry, and clear limits.
principles.test: Interrupt and reopen: recover the work without re-entering data or losing context.

principles.title: Serial position
principles.claim: Recall of a sequence can vary with position.
principles.when: Sequences of instructions or summaries that must be remembered.
principles.action: Try an orienting start, coherent grouping, and a close with the next action.
principles.avoid: Reordering expert navigation just to place items at the start or end.
principles.boundary: Free-recall studies do not prove a universal menu hierarchy.
principles.test: Separate a delayed-recall test from a search test with visible options.

principles.title: Contextual Hick–Hyman
principles.claim: Stimulus–response uncertainty can increase choice time.
principles.when: Ambiguous options or ones that are hard to tell apart.
principles.action: Improve names, grouping, relevance, and compatibility before removing capabilities.
principles.avoid: Cutting every menu to three options by formula.
principles.boundary: Practice, search, probabilities, and associations change the situation.
principles.test: Compare correct decisions, time, and detours for novice and expert users.

principles.title: Choice overload
principles.claim: The effect of many options depends on the task and on preferences.
principles.when: Catalogs or settings that are hard to compare.
principles.action: Ease comparison, filters, and justifiable suggested values.
principles.avoid: Mistaking catalog breadth for evidence of overload.
principles.boundary: Experts and people with clear preferences may need more options.
principles.test: Measure choice quality and abandonment by cohort, not only clicks.

principles.title: Mental models
principles.claim: The user's expectation can differ from the implementation model.
principles.when: Save, publish, export, or sync get confused.
principles.action: Name objects and actions in domain terms; explain scope and persistence.
principles.avoid: Using table, component, or internal process names as information architecture.
principles.boundary: Do not invent mental models from a fictional persona.
principles.test: Ask what they expect to happen before acting and compare with the result.

principles.title: Familiarity and learning
principles.claim: Conventions can transfer learning; novelty can serve a goal.
principles.when: Redesign or new product with unconventional interaction.
principles.action: Keep common semantics and justify breaks by task or expressive value.
principles.avoid: Cloning competitors or replacing everything with a generic template.
principles.boundary: Visual familiarity does not make up for behavior that differs from expectation.
principles.test: Compare first use, return, and expert execution.

principles.title: Framing and evaluator bias
principles.claim: How a decision is phrased can influence its evaluation.
principles.when: Tests, pricing, sensitive decisions, or design reports.
principles.action: Use neutral questions, counterbalanced order, and comparable alternatives.
principles.avoid: Steering participants toward the favorite design or hiding costs.
principles.boundary: A named bias does not diagnose individual behavior.
principles.test: Review script, order, and contradicting evidence before recommending.

principles.title: Occam and complexity bias
principles.claim: Preferring a sufficient explanation or solution with fewer assumptions is a working heuristic.
principles.when: A large system is proposed for localized friction.
principles.action: Compare a minimal sufficient solution with the complex alternative and its costs.
principles.avoid: Equating simple with fewer pixels or fewer capabilities.
principles.boundary: Less code does not mean less human effort or lower risk.
principles.test: Solve the same adverse scenario in both alternatives.

principles.title: Tesler: who carries the complexity
principles.claim: Making explicit who absorbs each difficulty helps design.
principles.when: Automation, forms, or professional tools.
principles.action: Assign each decision to the system or the person by context, cost, and authority.
principles.avoid: Calling it simplicity when uncertainty moves to the user or to an opaque AI.
principles.boundary: It is not a physical law; removing unnecessary requirements can reduce complexity.
principles.test: List the alternative's hidden decisions, failures, and recovery.

principles.title: Pareto without dropping critical cases
principles.claim: Observed frequency can guide priorities.
principles.when: There are too many journeys to research in one session.
principles.action: Prioritize impact, frequency, and severity; include rare high-harm failures.
principles.avoid: Assuming an exact 80/20 or excluding disability because of lower volume.
principles.boundary: Low frequency does not mean low value or acceptable harm.
principles.test: Publish coverage and exclusion reasons; keep severe risks visible.

principles.title: Parkinson as a work limit
principles.claim: An explicit limit can help bound research; it is not evidence of better interfaces.
principles.when: Exploration grows without a decision or a test.
principles.action: Set a question, budget, and reviewable exit criterion.
principles.avoid: Using artificial urgency against the user or cutting risk tests.
principles.boundary: Available time does not set the real complexity of the task.
principles.test: Close on sufficient evidence or record a blocker, not on meeting a quota.

principles.title: Robustness without ambiguity
principles.claim: Accepting safe variations does not mean guessing meaning.
principles.when: Inputs for dates, money, names, units, or imports.
principles.action: Normalize only unambiguous formats; show the interpretation and ask for a decision when it matters.
principles.avoid: Silently converting ambiguous dates, currencies, or permissions.
principles.boundary: A UX application of an engineering caution, not an experimental result about forms.
principles.test: Test hard local inputs and check that the semantic value does not change.

principles.title: Goal gradient
principles.claim: Getting closer to a reward can change effort in some contexts.
principles.when: A journey has real progress and a chosen goal.
principles.action: Show verifiable milestones and what remains without hiding requirements.
principles.avoid: Inventing progress, urgency, or penalties to force continuation.
principles.boundary: Results in rewards programs do not guarantee activation in all software.
principles.test: Compare useful completion, understanding, and regret.

principles.title: Honest endowed progress
principles.claim: Acknowledging real preparation can give initial orientation.
principles.when: Data or steps already legitimately completed exist.
principles.action: Show what was resolved, where it came from, and how to correct it.
principles.avoid: Marking fictional steps as done to exploit a bias.
principles.boundary: A studied technique can be inappropriate even if it raises conversion.
principles.test: The person must explain what is done and what they actually authorized.

principles.title: Zeigarnik and Ovsiankina
principles.claim: Recent evidence separates recall of tasks from the tendency to resume them.
principles.when: Interruptions, drafts, or reminders.
principles.action: Make it easy to return voluntarily with context preserved.
principles.avoid: Promising better memory or creating anxiety through perpetually unfinished tasks.
principles.boundary: The 2025 meta-analysis finds no general recall advantage for unfinished tasks.
principles.test: Measure recovery of work, not compulsion or longer sessions.

principles.title: Flow with an exit
principles.claim: Clear goals, continuity, and feedback are candidates to reduce work interruptions.
principles.when: Editing, creating, practicing, or long journeys.
principles.action: Keep context, offer discoverable shortcuts, and allow pausing without penalty.
principles.avoid: Equating flow with infinite scroll or maximizing captive time.
principles.boundary: Subjective fluency does not certify productivity or correct decisions.
principles.test: Observe continuity, errors, recovery, and sense of control.

principles.title: Peak–end without makeup
principles.claim: Retrospective evaluation can be sensitive to standout moments and the ending.
principles.when: End of a task, a major error, or confirmation of a result.
principles.action: Close with a verifiable result, consequences, and the next path.
principles.avoid: Compensating for a harmful journey with confetti or a pretty final screen.
principles.boundary: A pleasant memory does not prove correctness or accessibility.
principles.test: Separate retrospective evaluation, performance, and recovery.

principles.title: Learning while doing
principles.claim: Some people prioritize the immediate task over learning first.
principles.when: Onboarding or complex features.
principles.action: Let people start; offer a useful example, contextual help, and an expert path.
principles.avoid: Forcing long tours before delivering value.
principles.boundary: Dangerous tasks can require prior training or a check.
principles.test: Try an initial task without a tour, then repeat an advanced task.

principles.title: Aesthetics and perceived usability
principles.claim: Attractiveness and perceived ease can be related without guaranteeing success.
principles.when: A design gets praise but the flow still fails.
principles.action: Evaluate craft and task outcomes separately, keeping the visual identity.
principles.avoid: Using taste, modernity, or an aesthetic score to approve a blocker.
principles.boundary: Tolerance of minor defects does not fix severe errors.
principles.test: Contrast opinion, observable behavior, and recovery failures.

principles.title: Proximity
principles.claim: Visual closeness suggests a relationship.
principles.when: Labels, help, and controls are associated wrongly.
principles.action: Make spacing and alignment express real relationships.
principles.avoid: Moving a label away from its field or changing grouping by width without intent.
principles.boundary: Visual grouping and accessible reading order are different contracts.
principles.test: Check field association and linear reading at narrow width.

principles.title: Similarity
principles.claim: Similar elements suggest related functions or categories.
principles.when: Buttons, states, or list items use inconsistent languages.
principles.action: Keep one meaning per pattern and explicit variations per state.
principles.avoid: Making a decorative element look actionable.
principles.boundary: Consistency without state contrast also confuses.
principles.test: Ask people to predict what is interactive and how selection is shown.

principles.title: Common region
principles.claim: A container can make a group perceivable.
principles.when: Settings or results lack clear boundaries.
principles.action: Use containment for a real unit of task or information.
principles.avoid: Turning every line into a card and duplicating hierarchies.
principles.boundary: More surfaces can hinder scanning in dense tools.
principles.test: Compare locating information and associating actions.

principles.title: Continuity, connection, and figure–ground
principles.claim: Connections and layer separation can explain relationships and focus.
principles.when: Graphs, selection, panels, or overlapping elements.
principles.action: Connect only true relationships and keep names, order, and contrast.
principles.avoid: Relying only on lines, common motion, or visual closure to understand the system.
principles.boundary: Gestalt grouping is a design lens; it does not validate accessibility or graph comprehension.
principles.test: Read the result without color, without motion, and through a linear alternative.

principles.title: Fitts and motor effort
principles.claim: Distance and effective width influence pointing tasks under certain conditions.
principles.when: Small, separated, or imprecise actions.
principles.action: Improve hit area, spacing, and placement for mouse, touch, or assistive input.
principles.avoid: Enlarging only the drawing or applying a universal constant without reviewing exceptions.
principles.boundary: A motor model alone does not cover comprehension, search, or the danger of accidental activation.
principles.test: Measure hits and errors with the real input method.

principles.title: Recovery and reversibility
principles.claim: A task is not fully designed without its failure and recovery.
principles.when: Deletion, export, saving, import, or bulk changes.
principles.action: Prevent costly errors and offer idempotent retry, real undo, or explicit compensation.
principles.avoid: Promising undo when the backend cannot reverse consequences.
principles.boundary: Confirmation does not replace a safe model; do not ask for it on every trivial gesture.
principles.test: Cause a partial failure and check what persists, what repeats, and what can be reversed.

principles.title: Modes, selection, and scope
principles.claim: Actions must reveal which objects and which mode they operate on.
principles.when: Editors, creative tools, panels, and batch actions.
principles.action: Make selection, active tool, scope, and dirty or saved state visible.
principles.avoid: Hiding frequent controls in the name of minimalism.
principles.boundary: Useful information density can beat a sparse screen.
principles.test: Change mode and selection; predict and check the affected set.

principles.title: Keyboard, focus, and alternatives
principles.claim: Reviewing input, focus, and accessible equivalents requires interaction, not only screenshots.
principles.when: Controls, dialogs, dragging, or unconventional experiences.
principles.action: Offer a keyboard path, visible focus, and an alternative to dragging where it applies.
principles.avoid: Claiming conformance from a scanner or a screenshot.
principles.boundary: WCAG 2.2 has levels and exceptions; check the exact criterion.
principles.test: Run the task with the keyboard and available assistive technology; record what was not tested.

principles.title: Cognitive accessibility
principles.claim: Understanding, remembering, and recovering are explicit dimensions of inclusive design.
principles.when: Authentication, help, data entry, or complex instructions.
principles.action: Use plain language, persistent context, and aids that do not depend on remembering arbitrary codes.
principles.avoid: Attributing limits or preferences to a disability without research.
principles.boundary: COGA complements WCAG; it adds no automatic certification.
principles.test: Include relevant people and check autonomy, not only label reading.

principles.title: Difficult content and internationalization
principles.claim: Designing with real data means accepting variety of length, script, and context.
principles.when: Long names, plurals, dates, RTL, zoom, or mixed languages.
principles.action: Test edge content, logical order, units, and expansion; preserve meaning.
principles.avoid: Truncating the only identifying difference or interpreting an ambiguous date.
principles.boundary: Text direction, numbers, icons, and action order need separate decisions.
principles.test: Use long fixtures, zoom, and relevant locales in the affected flow.

principles.title: Delegation contract
principles.claim: Understanding and authorizing an action is different from asking for a suggestion.
principles.when: An AI acts on files, messages, accounts, or transactions.
principles.action: Separate proposal, scope, authorization, execution, and receipt; offer interruption with honest limits.
principles.avoid: Treating conversation or trust as unlimited permission.
principles.boundary: Design grants no capabilities or permissions the tool does not have.
principles.test: Try an unauthorized action, a scope change, cancellation, and partial failure.

principles.title: Calibrated trust and useful friction
principles.claim: Reducing overreliance can require review effort proportional to risk.
principles.when: Recommendations or decisions with consequences.
principles.action: Show origin, verifiable limits, and the ability to correct; ask for review where risk changes.
principles.avoid: Inventing confidence percentages or using a persuasive explanation as proof.
principles.boundary: More explanation or friction does not always improve the decision; it depends on the case.
principles.test: Measure acceptance of wrong results as well as satisfaction and speed.

principles.title: Stable adaptive UI
principles.claim: Adaptation must keep control and orientation, not rearrange the world without notice.
principles.when: Generative interfaces, recommendations, or panels that change with context.
principles.action: Keep anchors, selection, focus, and a manual path; allow rejecting and reverting adaptation.
principles.avoid: Moving the active button, changing permissions, or silently replacing preferences.
principles.boundary: It is a proposed contract, not a prediction of dominant interfaces in 2027.
principles.test: Trigger changes during a task and check continuity, focus, and recovery.

principles.title: Controllable memory and privacy
principles.claim: Keeping useful context requires the person to understand its scope.
principles.when: Memory, personalization, private files, or agent history.
principles.action: Explain what is used, where it comes from, and how to correct, exclude, or delete it when the capability exists.
principles.avoid: Promising total forgetting, local processing, or privacy the architecture does not guarantee.
principles.boundary: Do not infer consent across accounts, devices, or projects.
principles.test: Check context isolation and make controls match real effects.

principles.title: Asynchronous states and receipts
principles.claim: Generated text is not proof that an action completed.
principles.when: Agents, asset generation, and long-running jobs.
principles.action: Distinguish queued, running, waiting for a human, partial, cancelled, and verified final through real receipts.
principles.avoid: Showing success because the model narrated it, or percent progress without a denominator.
principles.boundary: Cancelling a request does not reverse effects that already happened.
principles.test: Cut the connection and repeat the request: do not duplicate effects or lose the partial result.

principles.title: Interaction and task latency
principles.claim: INP and total work duration describe different things.
principles.when: The interface responds slowly or a process takes long.
principles.action: Measure local feedback, first useful result, completion, and failures separately.
principles.avoid: Treating the historical 400 ms as a universal guarantee or mistaking streaming for finished work.
principles.boundary: Web percentiles do not certify productivity, nor do they apply the same way to a native process.
principles.test: Measure on real device and load, with declared percentiles and segments.

principles.title: Truthful progress
principles.claim: The indicator must represent real knowledge of the state.
principles.when: Imports, render, download, or generation.
principles.action: Use real counts when there is a denominator; otherwise describe the phase and available controls.
principles.avoid: Animating an invented percentage, blocking cancellation, or silently restarting work.
principles.boundary: An estimate must be labeled and correctable; do not promise an exact time.
principles.test: Simulate slowness, error, disconnection, and cancellation, checking messages and preserved work.

principles.title: Goal → signal → metric
principles.claim: Choosing a measure must start from a user goal.
principles.when: Someone asks to improve UX, activation, or productivity.
principles.action: Define primary outcome, harm indicator, segment, and decision criterion before measuring.
principles.avoid: Inventing percentage improvements or treating more time inside as universal success.
principles.boundary: A qualitative pilot does not estimate population effects or prove causality.
principles.test: Keep protocol, data, denominators, and interpretation limits.

principles.title: Semantic and portable visual system
principles.claim: Tokens can represent reusable decisions with stable meanings.
principles.when: Themes, density, accessibility, or several platforms.
principles.action: Use semantic roles, keep existing components, and validate the supported format on export.
principles.avoid: Migrating libraries only for fashion or calling DTCG a W3C Recommendation.
principles.boundary: The format guarantees neither good design nor interoperability with every tool.
principles.test: Check states, contrast, aliases, and fallback in real consumers.
